notes.definition: The cell cycle is the series of stages in which a cell grows, copies its DNA and then divides by mitosis to form two genetically identical cells. Mitosis is the stage in which one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides.
explanation: Cells divide in a series of stages called the cell cycle. During the cell cycle the genetic material is doubled and then divided equally between two identical daughter cells. AQA describes the cycle in three overall stages. You need to know these three stages and what happens in each, but you do not need to learn the names of the separate phases within mitosis.

Stage 1 is the longest stage. Before a cell can divide it needs to grow and increase the number of sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria, so that each new cell will have enough of them. The DNA replicates (is copied) to form two copies of each chromosome. After this, each chromosome is made of two identical copies joined together, which is why chromosomes look X-shaped in pictures of dividing cells.

Stage 2 is mitosis. The chromosomes line up and one set of chromosomes (one copy of each chromosome) is pulled to each end of the cell. The nucleus then divides, so a new nucleus forms at each end. Because the DNA was copied exactly in stage 1, each new nucleus receives exactly the same genetic information as the other, and the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell.

Stage 3 is the division of the cytoplasm and cell membrane. This forms two separate cells. The two daughter cells are genetically identical to each other and to the original parent cell, and they have the same number of chromosomes. In plant cells a new cell wall also forms between the two cells. Each daughter cell can then begin the cycle again, starting with growth.

Cell division by mitosis is important in the growth and development of multicellular organisms. It produces the extra cells needed when an organism grows, and it replaces cells that are damaged or worn out, for example when a cut in the skin heals or when red blood cells and skin cells are replaced. In plants, mitosis happens mainly in the meristems at the tips of roots and shoots. Mitosis is also used in asexual reproduction, because the offspring are genetically identical to the parent.

You may be asked to recognise where mitosis is occurring in a given context. Look for clues such as growth, repair, replacement of cells or the production of genetically identical cells. In micrographs of dividing tissue, such as an onion root tip, cells in mitosis are the ones with visible, thick chromosomes. Counting the proportion of cells in each stage lets you estimate how long each stage of the cycle lasts, because the proportion of cells in a stage is proportional to the time spent in that stage.
keyFacts: Cells divide in a series of stages called the cell cycle.
During the cell cycle the genetic material is doubled and then divided into two identical cells.
Stage 1: the cell grows, increases its number of sub-cellular structures (such as ribosomes and mitochondria) and replicates its DNA.
Stage 2 (mitosis): one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides.
Stage 3: the cytoplasm and cell membrane divide to form two identical cells.
Daughter cells have the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell (46 in humans).
Mitosis is needed for growth, development, repair and replacement of cells.
In plants, mitosis happens mainly in meristems at the tips of roots and shoots.
Stage 1 is the longest part of the cycle, so most cells seen in a tissue sample are in stage 1.
Percentage of cells in a stage ≈ percentage of the cycle time spent in that stage.

keyTerms.definition: The series of stages a cell goes through as it grows, copies its DNA and divides into two identical cells.
The stage of the cell cycle in which one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides.
The copying of DNA so that each chromosome has two identical copies before the cell divides.
The two new cells produced when a cell divides. After mitosis they are genetically identical to each other and to the parent cell.
Having exactly the same genes (the same DNA) as another cell.
The parts inside a cell, such as ribosomes, mitochondria and chloroplasts, whose number increases before a cell divides.
A region of a plant (root tip or shoot tip) where cells divide rapidly by mitosis.

equations.name: Percentage of cells in a stage
equations.formula: percentage of cells in a stage = (number of cells in that stage ÷ total number of cells counted) × 100

equations.name: Time spent in a stage
equations.formula: time in stage = (number of cells in that stage ÷ total number of cells counted) × total length of the cell cycle
equations.units: same unit as the cell cycle length (for example hours or minutes)

workedExamples.title: Percentage of cells in mitosis
workedExamples.question: A student counts 250 cells in an onion root tip. 20 of the cells are in mitosis. Calculate the percentage of cells in mitosis.

workedExamples.title: Estimating time spent in mitosis
workedExamples.question: In a root tip, 18 out of 300 cells are in mitosis. One complete cell cycle takes 20 hours. Estimate the time spent in mitosis in minutes.

workedExamples.question: A single animal cell has a cell cycle lasting 8 hours. Assuming every cell keeps dividing, how many cells will there be after 24 hours?
steps: Each cycle doubles the number of cells: 1 → 2 → 4 → 8.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think mitosis is the whole cell cycle.
misconceptions.right: In fact mitosis is only stage 2, where the nucleus divides. Growth and DNA replication happen before it, and the cytoplasm and membrane divide after it.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think daughter cells have half the number of chromosomes of the parent cell.
misconceptions.right: In fact the DNA is copied first, so each daughter cell gets a full set: the same number of chromosomes as the parent (46 in humans).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the cell divides straight away after it is formed.
misconceptions.right: In fact a cell must first grow and increase its number of sub-cellular structures such as ribosomes and mitochondria, which takes most of the cycle.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the two daughter cells are only similar to the parent cell.
misconceptions.right: In fact they are genetically identical to each other and to the parent cell (unless a rare mutation occurs).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think mitosis is used to make gametes.
misconceptions.right: In fact mitosis makes body cells for growth, repair and replacement. Gametes are made by a different type of division, which halves the chromosome number.

realWorld: When you cut your skin, cells around the wound divide by mitosis to replace the damaged cells and close the wound.
Cancer is caused by changes in cells that lead to uncontrolled growth and division. Many chemotherapy drugs work by stopping cells completing the cell cycle.
Gardeners take cuttings from plants; cells in the cutting divide by mitosis to grow new roots, producing plants genetically identical to the parent.
Bone marrow cells divide by mitosis constantly to replace the millions of red blood cells that wear out every second.
examTips: Learn the three stages in order and what happens in each: (1) growth, more ribosomes and mitochondria, DNA replicates; (2) mitosis, one set of chromosomes to each end, nucleus divides; (3) cytoplasm and cell membrane divide.
Always use the word 'identical' when describing the cells produced by mitosis, and say they have the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell.
You do not need the names of the phases of mitosis. Do not waste time writing them; describe what happens instead.
In 'time in stage' calculations, divide the number of cells in that stage by the total, then multiply by the cycle length. Check the units the question asks for (hours or minutes).
When asked why a cell must grow before dividing, mention increasing the number of sub-cellular structures so each daughter cell has enough.
summary: The cell cycle has three stages: growth and DNA replication, mitosis, then division of the cytoplasm and membrane.
Before dividing, a cell grows, makes more ribosomes and mitochondria and copies its DNA.
In mitosis one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides.
Two genetically identical daughter cells are produced, each with the same chromosome number as the parent.
Mitosis is essential for growth, development, repair and replacement of cells.
The proportion of cells in a stage can be used to estimate how long that stage lasts.

flashcards.front: What happens in stage 1 of the cell cycle?
flashcards.back: The cell grows, increases the number of sub-cellular structures (such as ribosomes and mitochondria) and the DNA replicates.
One set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell and the nucleus divides.

flashcards.front: What happens in stage 3 of the cell cycle?
flashcards.back: The cytoplasm and cell membrane divide to form two identical cells.

flashcards.front: Why must DNA replicate before mitosis?
flashcards.back: So that there are two copies of each chromosome and each daughter cell receives a full, identical set.

flashcards.front: How many chromosomes are in each daughter cell after mitosis of a human body cell?
flashcards.back: 46, the same as the parent cell.

flashcards.front: How do daughter cells from mitosis compare genetically with the parent?
flashcards.back: They are genetically identical to each other and to the parent.

flashcards.front: Give three reasons why mitosis is important.
flashcards.back: Growth, development, and repair or replacement of damaged or worn-out cells.

flashcards.front: Where does mitosis mainly happen in plants?
flashcards.back: In meristems at the tips of roots and shoots.

flashcards.front: Which stage of the cell cycle is the longest?
Why do chromosomes look X-shaped before mitosis?
flashcards.back: The DNA has replicated and the two identical copies are still joined together.

flashcards.front: How do you estimate the time spent in mitosis from a cell count?
flashcards.back: (cells in mitosis ÷ total cells) × length of the whole cell cycle.

questions.question: What is produced when a cell divides by mitosis?
options: Four cells that are all genetically different
Two cells that are genetically identical
Two cells with half the number of chromosomes
markScheme: 1 mark: two genetically identical cells
questions.explanation: Mitosis produces two daughter cells that are genetically identical to each other and to the parent cell. Four genetically different cells with half the chromosomes describes the division that makes gametes, not mitosis.

options: One set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell
markScheme: 1 mark: the DNA replicates
questions.explanation: In stage 1 the cell grows, makes more sub-cellular structures and copies its DNA. Division of the nucleus and pulling chromosomes apart happen in stage 2 (mitosis); the cytoplasm divides in stage 3.

questions.question: Which process does NOT involve mitosis?
options: Healing of a cut on the skin
Making sperm cells in the testes
markScheme: 1 mark: making sperm cells in the testes
questions.explanation: Gametes such as sperm are made by a different type of cell division that halves the chromosome number. Growth, repair and replacement all use mitosis.

questions.question: What is the final stage of the cell cycle?
options: The cytoplasm and cell membrane divide
markScheme: 1 mark: the cytoplasm and cell membrane divide
questions.explanation: Stage 3, the final stage, is the division of the cytoplasm and cell membrane to form two separate cells. The nucleus divides earlier, in mitosis.

questions.question: Before a cell divides it increases the number of some sub-cellular structures. Which pair of structures does it increase?
markScheme: 1 mark: ribosomes and mitochondria
questions.explanation: The cell makes more ribosomes and mitochondria so each daughter cell has enough. Cells do not make a second nucleus in stage 1; plasmids and flagella are features of bacteria.

questions.question:
A cell from a mouse has 40 chromosomes. The cell divides by mitosis.
How many chromosomes are in each daughter cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: 40
questions.explanation: The DNA is copied before mitosis and one full set goes to each daughter cell, so each has the same number as the parent: 40. 20 would be the number in a gamete.

options: Most cells in root tips have stopped dividing completely
The stain used kills cells in mitosis
Stage 1 of the cell cycle takes much longer than mitosis
markScheme: 1 mark: stage 1 takes much longer than mitosis
questions.explanation: The proportion of cells in a stage reflects how long that stage lasts. Growth and DNA replication take most of the cycle, so most cells are seen in stage 1 at any one moment.

questions.question: A drug stops DNA replication. What is the most likely effect on cells treated with this drug?
options: They cannot complete the cell cycle and divide
They produce daughter cells with double the chromosome number
markScheme: 1 mark: they cannot complete the cell cycle and divide
questions.explanation: Without two copies of each chromosome a cell cannot give a full set to each daughter cell, so the cycle stops. This is one way that some anti-cancer drugs slow down dividing cells.

questions.question: Which sequence correctly shows the amount of DNA in one cell through one cell cycle, starting just after the cell is formed?
options: Doubles, then halves when the cell divides
markScheme: 1 mark: doubles, then halves when the cell divides
questions.explanation: The DNA doubles when it replicates in stage 1. When the cell divides, each daughter cell receives half of this doubled amount, which is the same as the original amount.

questions.question:
A plant cell contains 24 chromosomes. The cell divides by mitosis.
How many chromosomes are in each daughter cell?
markScheme: 1 mark: 24
questions.explanation: Mitosis gives daughter cells with the same number of chromosomes as the parent cell.

questions.question:
A student counted the cells in a root tip.
Table 1 shows the results.
Calculate the percentage of cells that were in mitosis.
questions.explanation: 32 ÷ 400 = 0.08, and 0.08 × 100 = 8%. Check: 10% of 400 is 40, so 32 is a bit less than 10%.

questions.question:
A single cell has a cell cycle lasting 12 hours. Every new cell also divides every 12 hours.
Calculate the number of cells there will be after 48 hours.
markScheme: 1 mark: 48 ÷ 12 = 4 cycles
1 mark: 2⁴ = 16 cells
questions.explanation: There are 4 cycles. The number doubles each cycle: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. A common error is 1 × 4 = 4 or 2 × 4 = 8, which treats doubling as adding.

questions.question:
A scientist studied some cells.
Table 1 shows the results.
The percentage of cells in mitosis is the same as the percentage of the cell cycle spent in mitosis.
Estimate how long mitosis lasts in these cells.
Give your answer in minutes.

rows: Length of one cell cycle in hours

markScheme: 1 mark: = 1.6 hours
1 mark: 1.6 × 60 = 96 minutes
questions.explanation: The percentage of cells in a stage matches the percentage of time spent in it. 8% of 20 hours = 1.6 hours. 1.6 × 60 = 96 minutes. Check: 10% of 20 h is 2 h (120 min), and 8% is a little less.

questions.question:
A scientist counted the cells in each stage of the cell cycle in an onion root tip.
Table 1 shows the results.
One cell cycle takes 16 hours.
Calculate the time spent in mitosis.
Give your answer in minutes.
markScheme: 1 mark: total = 150 cells
1 mark: × 60 = 160 minutes
questions.explanation: Total cells = 120 + 25 + 5 = 150. Fraction in mitosis = 25 ÷ 150 = 0.1667. Time = 0.1667 × 16 h = 2.667 h = 160 minutes. A common mistake is to divide by 120 instead of by the total.

questions.question: State one reason why multicellular organisms need cells to divide by mitosis.
markScheme: 1 mark: any one of growth / development / repair of damaged tissue / replacement of cells
questions.explanation: Mitosis produces new identical cells for growth and development and to repair or replace damaged and worn-out cells.

questions.question:
Figure 1 shows a cell at the start of mitosis.
Describe what happens to the chromosomes and the nucleus during mitosis.

acceptedAnswers: one set of chromosomes pulled to each end
markScheme: 1 mark: one set of chromosomes is pulled to each end of the cell
1 mark: the nucleus divides
questions.explanation: In mitosis the copies of each chromosome are separated, with one set pulled to each end of the cell, and the nucleus divides into two.

questions.question: Name the part of a plant where cells divide rapidly by mitosis.
markScheme: 1 mark: meristem / root tip / shoot tip
questions.explanation: Meristems at the tips of roots and shoots are where most plant cell division happens.

questions.question: Explain why a cell must increase its number of mitochondria and ribosomes before it divides.
markScheme: 1 mark: the structures are shared between the two daughter cells
1 mark: so each daughter cell has enough mitochondria for respiration / ribosomes for protein synthesis
questions.explanation: When the cytoplasm divides, the sub-cellular structures are shared out. Without making more first, each daughter cell would have too few to release energy or make proteins.

questions.question: Explain why the two cells produced by mitosis are genetically identical.
acceptedAnswers: one copy of each chromosome goes to each cell
markScheme: 1 mark: the DNA is replicated / copied exactly to form two copies of each chromosome
1 mark: one copy of each chromosome goes to each daughter cell / one set to each end
questions.explanation: Because each chromosome is copied exactly and one copy goes into each new nucleus, both cells receive the same genetic information.

questions.question: A child falls and grazes her knee. Two weeks later the skin has healed. Suggest how cell division was involved in the healing.
markScheme: 1 mark: skin cells divided by mitosis
1 mark: to produce new (identical) skin cells to replace the damaged ones / repair the tissue
questions.explanation: Repair of damaged tissue is a key use of mitosis. Cells near the wound divide to make genetically identical skin cells that fill the gap.

questions.question:
A student says:
'In mitosis the chromosomes are shared out, so each new cell gets half of the parent cell's chromosomes.'
Explain why the student is wrong.
markScheme: 1 mark: the DNA replicates before mitosis / each chromosome is copied
1 mark: so each daughter cell receives a full set / the same number of chromosomes as the parent
questions.explanation: The copying in stage 1 doubles the genetic material. Mitosis then divides this doubled material in half, giving each cell the original full amount.

questions.question: A scientist wants to find which stage of the cell cycle takes longest in some root tip cells. Describe how she could use a stained slide of root tip cells to do this.
acceptedAnswers: proportion of cells relates to time
markScheme: 1 mark: count the number of cells in each stage in a field of view
1 mark: count a large sample / several fields of view
1 mark: the stage with the most cells / highest proportion of cells lasts the longest
questions.explanation: The fraction of cells in each stage is proportional to the time spent in that stage, so the stage containing the most cells is the longest. A large sample makes the estimate more reliable.

questions.question: Strawberry plants produce runners that grow into new plants. The new plants are genetically identical to the parent. Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: the cells of the new plant are produced by mitosis
1 mark: so they have identical DNA / no gametes fuse so no mixing of genetic information
questions.explanation: The runner and the new plant grow by mitosis from the parent's cells, so they carry exact copies of the parent's DNA.

questions.question: State what happens to the DNA in stage 1 of the cell cycle.
markScheme: 1 mark: it replicates / is copied (forming two copies of each chromosome)
questions.explanation: The DNA replicates so that each chromosome has two identical copies ready to be separated in mitosis.

questions.question: Describe the stages of the cell cycle, starting with a newly formed cell and ending with two new cells.
markScheme: Indicative content: stage 1: cell grows; number of sub-cellular structures increases; for example ribosomes and mitochondria; DNA replicates; two copies of each chromosome. Stage 2 (mitosis): chromosomes line up; one set of chromosomes pulled to each end of the cell; nucleus divides. Stage 3: cytoplasm divides; cell membrane divides; two daughter cells formed; genetically identical to each other and to the parent; same number of chromosomes as the parent.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): all three stages described in the correct order with detail in each, including DNA replication and identical daughter cells.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): at least two stages described correctly in order, with some detail.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements about cell division, for example 'the cell grows then splits', with little detail or incorrect order.
questions.explanation: A full-mark answer covers all three stages in order with the key words: grows, ribosomes and mitochondria, DNA replicates, one set of chromosomes to each end, nucleus divides, cytoplasm and membrane divide, two identical cells.

questions.question:
A scientist counted the number of cells in mitosis in two root tips, A and B.
Root tip A came from a seedling grown at 20 °C. Root tip B came from a seedling grown at 30 °C.
Table 1 shows the results.
Compare the results and suggest an explanation.
Use calculations in your answer.
markScheme: Indicative content: A = 6 ÷ 200 × 100 = 3%; B = 18 ÷ 200 × 100 = 9%; B has three times the percentage of cells in mitosis; cells divide more often / faster at 30 °C; reactions controlled by enzymes (for example DNA replication) are faster at higher temperature; so root tip B is likely to grow faster; only one root tip at each temperature so results may not be repeatable; need to repeat and keep other variables constant.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): correct percentages calculated and compared, with a plausible explanation linked to the rate of cell division and a comment on reliability.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple comparison (for example 'B has more cells in mitosis') with limited or no calculation or explanation.
questions.explanation: Converting to percentages (3% and 9%) makes the comparison fair. More cells in mitosis suggests more frequent division and faster growth at 30 °C, probably because enzyme-controlled processes are faster. A single sample at each temperature limits confidence.

questions.question: Which word describes the genetic relationship between the two daughter cells made by mitosis?
markScheme: 1 mark: identical
questions.explanation: The daughter cells are genetically identical to each other and to the parent cell.

questions.question: Which of these cells would you expect to divide by mitosis most often?
options: A skin cell next to a healing cut
A nerve cell in the brain of an adult
markScheme: 1 mark: a skin cell next to a healing cut
questions.explanation: Skin cells next to a wound divide rapidly by mitosis to repair the damage. Adult nerve cells rarely divide, red blood cells have no nucleus, and mature xylem cells are dead.
